History:
• Presenting complaint: Mild difficulty breathing and concern for possible allergic reaction after insect (bee/wasp) sting.  
• Onset/duration: Sting occurred “a few minutes ago” prior to call; breathing feels “not particularly acute” but patient anxious it may worsen.  
• Local reaction: Small puncture mark with mild redness/blotchiness on right arm; no significant swelling reported.  
• Systemic symptoms: Sensation of slight lip swelling (right side) and “tongue feels a bit weird,” but no visible swelling, no stridor, no voice change, no throat tightness, no dizziness, no GI symptoms.  
• Previous episodes: No prior anaphylaxis; never prescribed an epinephrine autoinjector.  
• Triggers: Recent single sting; no known other triggers.  
• Associated factors: Anxiety/panic tendency; patient lives alone, owns a cat.

Past Medical History:
• Eczema (past).  
• Occasional anxiety/panic attacks (never medicated).  
• Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not discussed).  
• Medications: None currently; no antihistamines taken yet.  

Physical Examination (video assessment):
• General: Alert, speaking in full sentences, no visible respiratory distress.  
• Airway: Lips and oral cavity appear normal; no swelling, no uvular/tonsillar edema; patient phonates “ah” without difficulty.  
• Respiratory: Breathing appears normal; no audible stridor or wheeze.  
• Skin: Right arm shows small puncture mark with mild erythema, no significant swelling or heat.  
• Other: No facial swelling observed.

Impression:
Localized allergic reaction to insect sting with anxiety; no current evidence of systemic anaphylaxis.

Management Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Start oral antihistamine—e.g., chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet, dose/route/frequency as instructed (one tablet up to 6 times/day) OR once-daily non-sedating antihistamine—over-the-counter.  
• Education: Provided verbal and written information on signs of anaphylaxis (lip/tongue swelling, stridor, breathing difficulty, rapid progression).  
• Safety-netting: If any deterioration (breathing difficulty, swelling, spreading rash, fever, redness/hot arm) go directly to Accident & Emergency (A&E) or call emergency services.  
• Infection precaution: If local area becomes hot, increasingly red, or spreads, will require evaluation for possible antibiotic therapy.  
• Follow-up: Re-contact primary care or telehealth service if symptoms worsen or for recurrent episodes; consider allergy testing only if reactions become frequent.

Patient Summary:
27-year-old male stung on right arm minutes before consult, developed mild localized rash and subjective lip sensation without objective airway compromise. Video exam showed stable airway and mild local erythema. Managed conservatively with oral antihistamine and strict return precautions.

Key Takeaways:
1. Start an over-the-counter antihistamine today and continue as directed.  
2. Seek immediate emergency care if breathing worsens, lips/tongue swell, or rash rapidly spreads.  
3. Monitor sting site for increasing redness, heat, or pus; seek review if these appear.

Next Steps:
• Obtain and take antihistamine as soon as possible.  
• Observe closely for at least several hours; if stable, no routine appointment required.  
• Re-evaluate with primary care if recurrent stings or allergic symptoms warrant further investigation.
